explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The burnt offering stays on the hearth of the altar all night, and God says "the fire must be kept burning on the altar." Then in verse 13 He says it again: "The fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it must not be extinguished." Said twice in a few verses, so nobody walks away confused.

explanations.answer: It must be put out at night
explanations.explanation: Close, but the text says the opposite. The burnt offering remains on the altar all night, and the fire is kept burning. In verse 13 God says, "it must not be extinguished." Putting a fire out at night is like switching my oven off with a full tray inside. You wake up to a very sad tray.

explanations.answer: It must be lit fresh each morning
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but a fresh light would mean the fire went out first. The text says the fire on the altar "must not be extinguished" (Leviticus 6:12). Each morning the priest adds wood to the fire that's already burning. I keep my ovens warm for the same kind of reason: starting cold puts you behind.

explanations.answer: As a pleasing aroma to the LORD
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The priest burns the memorial portion on the altar "as a pleasing aroma to the LORD." That handful is fine flour and olive oil, with all the frankincense. The text names the aroma as the purpose, and it doesn't add any other.

explanations.answer: To pay what the giver owes
explanations.explanation: This one sounds reasonable, but the text doesn't say it. Verse 15 says the memorial portion is burned "as a pleasing aroma to the LORD." Nothing in these verses mentions a debt being paid. Sometimes the answer is simply what the verse says, and it's a good habit to stick to that.

explanations.answer: To keep the altar fire going
explanations.explanation: The fire does have to keep going, but that's a different job. Verse 12 says the priest adds wood every morning to keep it burning. The grain offering's memorial portion is burned "as a pleasing aroma to the LORD." Think of wood as the fuel and the handful as the offering.
That's the word, friend. "Aaron and his sons are to eat the remainder." It's eaten without leaven in a holy place, the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Lunch with a view of the altar.

I get the thought, but nobody's stocking a pantry here. Verse 16 says Aaron and his sons are to eat the remainder. It must be eaten without leaven in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Eating is the instruction.

No price tag and no clearance rack here, friend. The text says "Aaron and his sons are to eat the remainder." It's eaten in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, in a holy place, and without leaven. The remainder goes straight from the altar to the priests' table.

Yes, baker. "Every grain offering for a priest shall be burned completely; it is not to be eaten." This is the one Aaron and his sons present on the day Aaron is anointed, half in the morning and half in the evening. So the priests eat the remainder of the people's grain offerings, but not their own.

explanations.answer: It is eaten by the high priest
explanations.explanation: Nobody eats this one. Verse 23 says every grain offering for a priest "is not to be eaten." It "shall be burned completely." It stays on the altar from start to finish, and no one takes any of it home.

explanations.answer: It is shared with the people
explanations.explanation: No sharing on this one, friend. Verse 23 says the priest's grain offering "shall be burned completely; it is not to be eaten." The whole thing goes on the altar. There's no plate for anyone.

That's right, baker. "The priest who offers it shall eat it." He eats it in a holy place, the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. And the text calls the sin offering most holy, so this is no ordinary meal.

Verse 26 says the opposite: "The priest who offers it shall eat it." It must be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Verse 29 adds that any male among the priests may eat it. It's most holy.

Right, friend. "The clay pot in which the sin offering is boiled must be broken." If it's boiled in a bronze pot instead, "the pot must be scoured and rinsed with water." I've dropped a pan or two in my day, but this is the one time breaking a pot is the instructions.

explanations.answer: It must be kept in the Tent
explanations.explanation: Not quite. The text never sends the pot to the Tent. Verse 28 says the clay pot "must be broken." A bronze pot gets scoured and rinsed with water instead.

explanations.answer: It must be given to the priest
explanations.explanation: There's no pot handoff in this verse, friend. The text says a clay pot used to boil the sin offering "must be broken." Only a bronze pot is kept, and it must be scoured and rinsed with water. The clay one doesn't make it to the end of the day.

Careful, baker, this is the twist in the verse. Any male among the priests may eat the sin offering, but verse 30 says there's an exception. "No sin offering may be eaten if its blood has been brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it must be burned." So it can't be eaten in that case.

That's right, friend. Verse 30 says, "no sin offering may be eaten if its blood has been brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it must be burned." The rule that any male among the priests may eat it has this one exception. It's a small clause, but it changes everything.

That's it, baker. "The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both." Both are most holy, both are eaten by the priests in a holy place, and both are slaughtered where the burnt offering is slaughtered. One law covers the two.

Not this one, friend. The peace offering gets its own law starting in verse 11. Verse 7 says, "The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both." Different offerings, different rules, and this pair shares one.

The grain offering has its own law, back in Leviticus 6:14. Here, verse 7 says "The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both." It names the sin offering, and that's the match.

I know it's tempting, but verse 18 says otherwise. If any of the meat is eaten on the third day, "it will not be accepted." It will not be credited to the one who presented it, and the one who eats it "shall bear his iniquity." Day three is a hard stop.

That's right, friend. Verse 18 says meat eaten on the third day "will not be accepted." It "will not be credited to the one who presented it." Verse 17 says anything left until the third day must be burned up.

explanations.answer: That person is cut off from his people
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "If anyone who is unclean eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people." Verse 21 says the same about someone who touches something unclean and then eats the meat. It's a serious one, so I'll just say plainly that this part is heavy.

explanations.answer: That person must pay back a fifth more
explanations.explanation: That's not what verse 20 gives. It says an unclean person who eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD "must be cut off from his people." No payment is named here. It's a heavy line, so I'll keep it plain.

explanations.answer: That person must wash and wait till evening
explanations.explanation: Washing and waiting aren't what this verse names. It says an unclean person who eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD "must be cut off from his people." Verse 21 repeats it for someone who touched something unclean and then ate. This is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "Speak to the Israelites and say, 'You are not to eat any of the fat of an ox, a sheep, or a goat.'" Up to now the laws were mostly for the priests. This one goes to the whole camp, like a message that lands in everyone's group chat.
Close, because most of this passage is for Aaron and his sons. But verse 23 says "Speak to the Israelites and say." So the fat command goes to everyone, not just the priests.
The elders aren't mentioned here, friend. Verse 23 says the LORD tells Moses, "Speak to the Israelites and say." So the command is for all the Israelites. No middle manager needed.

You've got it, baker. "The priest is to burn the fat on the altar, but the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons." The one who brings the offering carries it with his own hands and waves the breast before the LORD. Then the breast goes to Aaron and his sons.
He does carry it and wave it, which makes this one tricky. But verse 31 says, "the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons." It's the priests' portion.

Gatekeepers don't show up in these verses, friend. Verse 31 says "the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons." Verse 34 calls it a permanent portion from the sons of Israel. The text gives it to the priests.

That's right, friend. "The son of Aaron who presents the blood and fat of the peace offering shall have the right thigh as a portion." Verse 32 says the people give the right thigh to the priest as a contribution from their peace offering. The breast goes to Aaron and his sons, and the right thigh goes to the priest who presents the offering.

Verse 33 says the opposite. "The son of Aaron who presents the blood and fat of the peace offering shall have the right thigh as a portion." Verse 32 says you are to give the right thigh to the priest as a contribution from your peace offering. So the right thigh goes to that priest.

explanations.answer: Present their offerings to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Perfect, baker. Verse 38 says the LORD gave these laws to Moses on Mount Sinai "on the day He commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai." That sums up the whole stretch of laws. It's good to end where the text ends.
That's not what verse 38 says. It says that day, the LORD "commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai." Nothing about resting shows up in that verse.

The Passover isn't mentioned in these verses, friend. Verse 38 says the LORD commanded the Israelites "to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai." That's the command for that day on Mount Sinai.
